title: Why Sending Students To The Principal Is A Mistake
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that, outside of genuinely dangerous situations — violence, weapons, drugs, severe bullying — sending a student to the principal's office is a strategic mistake rather than a neutral disciplinary option. His central claim is that outsourcing discipline announces to the entire class that "the buck doesn't stop with you," which invites more brazen misbehavior and less respect, since students recalibrate their view of the teacher as someone who can't handle them without outside help. He extends the argument to the teacher's standing with administration, claiming that even if a principal says nothing critical aloud, needing repeated behavioral help quietly raises concern and can put a teacher on an improvement-plan radar. He also frames the psychological cost directly: relying on outside help erodes a teacher's own confidence and hands leverage over to students, leaving the teacher reduced to convincing, bribing, or begging for cooperation. The concrete solution offered is to become genuinely expert in classroom management through SCM's plan guides and books, framed as removing the need for outside intervention entirely, regardless of school, grade level, or roster.
points: Only genuine safety issues — violence, weapons, drugs, severe bullying — are said to justify sending a student to the office.
Outsourcing discipline is said to announce to the class that "the buck doesn't stop with you," inviting more misbehavior.
Repeated requests for administrative help with behavior are said to quietly damage a teacher's standing with the principal.
The proposed fix is to build genuine classroom management expertise rather than relying on outside intervention.
quotes: Beyond this, however, sending students to the office is a mistake.
It all but screams to that student and the rest of your class that you can’t handle them and therefore must call upon a real authority figure.
Any show of weakness in leadership, including inconsistency, bribery, and fear of giving consequences, is always followed by less respect for you.
It tells them they need to be concerned about you, keep an eye on you, and consider you for an improvement plan.
Effective classroom management isn’t magic. It isn’t trickery or manipulation.
By learning the SCM approach, you’ll never need outside help with any student or any class.
